last_attempts_log.asr_text: Space security news often uses one phrase for very different things: weapons in space. That phrase came into focus on September 14th, 2026. U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the United States was deploying orbital space control weapons to protect U.S. forces from hostile actions. An official U.S. Space Force article called this the first public acknowledgment that the Space Force had deployed weapons in space, but the statement did not name the systems or explain how they could attack another satellite. No target was identified. The wider term is counterspace. A 2025 U.S. Space Force framework uses that term for actions in orbit, through communication links, and on the ground. It can include physical attacks, electronic interference, and cyber operations.

last_attempts_log.asr_text: That means the current picture is mixed. In 2024, the Pentagon said a Russian satellite had been placed in a similar orbit to a U.S. government satellite and was likely able to attack other satellites, but no attack was confirmed. In December 2025, one report also described an alleged Russian plan to use small satellites and pellets against Starlink. The information could not be independently confirmed, and it was unclear whether the system had been tested or deployed. So the important change is not that every counter-space activity is new, it is that the United States has now openly acknowledged one category of weapon being placed in orbit.

That distinction matters. China's 2007, India's 2019 and Russia's 2021 anti-satellite missile tests were launched from Earth, not stationed in orbit. A 2022 cyberattack on Viasat's KA-SAT network disrupted users but did not destroy the satellite. The Pentagon's 2024 assessment also did not confirm an attack. The new U.S. statement describes a different kind of activity and acknowledged orbital deployment.

The legal picture is narrower than the technology picture. The Outer Space Treaty bans nuclear weapons and other mass destruction weapons in orbit and prohibits installing such weapons on the moon and other celestial bodies. It also requires space activity to follow international law, but it does not completely ban every conventional anti-satellite missile, jammer, or cyber operation. United Nations votes in 2024 and 2025 supported existing principles and further arms control work, but they did not create a new comprehensive treaty. The U.S. pledge against destructive direct-assent tests remains a national policy commitment.
